chunks: MOSFET terminals and their roles. The question: What are the terminals?
A MOSFET has four terminals: gate, drain, source and body. The gate is the control, and a voltage on it decides whether current can flow from drain to source.
It does that by creating or removing the channel, a thin conducting path between drain and source. The body is the silicon the channel forms in.
On discrete parts the body is wired to the source inside the package, which is why you usually see only three pins.
Think of a garden hose with a pinch valve. Water enters at the source, leaves at the drain, and the gate is a hand squeezing the hose from the outside through a thin wall.
The hand never touches the water, and it takes no flow to hold the squeeze. The body is the ground the hose lies on.
The analogy breaks down on one point: the hand here is an electric field, not a push.
Lateral NMOS. The gate is separated from the body by a thin oxide (grey), so it couples only through an electric field.
Source and drain are identical N+ islands; the body is the P-type silicon underneath. With enough gate voltage, an N-type inversion layer (dashed) bridges source and drain.
Gate: the control terminal, insulated by a thin oxide, so it draws almost no DC current. Source: where the charge carriers enter the channel. Voltages are measured from it.
Drain: where the carriers leave the channel. Body (bulk, substrate): the silicon under the channel.
Threshold voltage ( V t ): the gate-to-source voltage where the channel starts to form.
Take an NFET with its source on ground and an LED and resistor from the supply to its drain. Say its threshold is about 2 volts.
With the gate at 0 volts, no channel forms and the LED is off. Raise the gate to 5 volts, the channel forms, current flows from drain to source, and the LED lights.
The gate itself carries almost no current. That is the whole idea.
"Four terminals: gate, drain, source and body. The gate is insulated by the oxide, draws no DC current, and its voltage relative to the source creates or removes the channel.
The source supplies the carriers and is the reference for V GS and V DS . The drain collects them and usually connects to the load. The body is the silicon the channel lives in.
Discrete parts tie it to the source internally, which is why they have three pins and a body diode."
